question.text: Which of the following best describes the "distributable surplus" from which IDCW can be declared by a mutual fund scheme?

answer.text: It includes distributable reserves based on accrued income/expenses and realised gains, excludes valuation gains, and adjusts for valuation losses, so that IDCW is paid from real and realised profits
It is limited only to the interest income and dividend income received by the scheme
It includes only the realized capital gains from the sale of securities
It is the total NAV appreciation since the scheme's inception

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the NISM Series V-A workbook (pp.149, 150, 153), distributable reserves for IDCW are computed on an accrual basis of income and expenses and include realised gains. Unrealised (valuation) gains are EXCLUDED and valuation losses are ADJUSTED, so that IDCW is paid from real and realised profits, not from notional appreciation. The Trap: Limiting "distributable surplus" only to income actually received misses accrued income/realised capital gains. Limiting it to only realised capital gains misses income. Treating it as total NAV appreciation since inception ignores the workbook's exclusion of valuation gains and adjustment for valuation losses. Note: When a scheme declares a large IDCW, check whether it has adequate distributable surplus on this basis. Schemes that consistently pay IDCW out of proportion to accrued income and realised gains may effectively be returning capital, eroding the NAV over time.
